clinicalPearls: DIC is never a primary disease; it is always secondary to an underlying disorder such as sepsis, major trauma, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe (abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, retained products), severe pancreatitis or extensive burns, and treating the trigger is the single most important intervention.
There is simultaneous systemic activation of coagulation and fibrinolysis, so patients may present with bleeding, with microvascular and macrovascular thrombosis, or with both at once.

The characteristic laboratory picture is a falling platelet count, prolonged prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times, a low or falling fibrinogen and markedly raised D-dimer or fibrin degradation products.
The trend of serial results is far more informative than any single value; repeat testing over hours guides both diagnosis and component replacement.
The ISTH scoring system, applied only when a compatible clinical setting is present, helps to separate overt (decompensated) from non-overt DIC.
The blood film usually shows some fragmented red cells (schistocytes), but fragmentation is typically less florid than in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Management is largely supportive and directed at the cause; blood component replacement is reserved for active bleeding or a high bleeding risk rather than for correcting numbers alone.
A chronic, compensated form (classically with adenocarcinoma, giant haemangioma or a retained dead fetus) may present with thrombosis or migratory thrombophlebitis rather than bleeding.
reference.pathophysiology: DIC arises when a systemic stimulus, most often the release of tissue factor from injured or activated cells or from tumour, drives unregulated generation of thrombin throughout the microcirculation. Widespread thrombin activity converts fibrinogen to fibrin, deposits fibrin in small vessels and consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they can be replaced. Natural anticoagulant pathways (antithrombin, protein C and tissue factor pathway inhibitor) are overwhelmed and depleted, and endothelial injury with impaired fibrinolytic regulation compounds the process. The resulting intravascular fibrin causes microvascular occlusion and organ dysfunction, mechanical fragmentation of red cells produces a microangiopathic haemolytic picture, and secondary reactive fibrinolysis generates large amounts of fibrin degradation products that themselves impair haemostasis. The net clinical effect is a paradoxical combination of thrombosis and consumptive bleeding.
additionalDifferentials: HELLP syndrome and other pregnancy-associated coagulopathies
vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect
additionalInvestigations: prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time
fibrinogen level (interpreted as a trend, since it is an acute phase reactant)
blood film for schistocytes and thrombocytopenia
ISTH DIC score in a compatible clinical context
investigations directed at the trigger (blood cultures and septic screen, imaging, obstetric assessment)
redFlags: spontaneous bleeding from multiple unrelated sites including venepuncture and cannula sites
purpura fulminans or rapidly spreading skin necrosis
acral cyanosis or digital ischaemia progressing to gangrene
new organ dysfunction (oliguria, hypoxaemia, altered consciousness)
rapidly falling fibrinogen and platelet count on serial testing
reference.prognosis: Outcome is dominated by the underlying cause and the degree of organ failure, and mortality is high when DIC complicates sepsis or multi-organ dysfunction. Prompt reversal of the trigger and supportive haematological care allow recovery when the precipitant is treatable.
pitfalls: relying on a single set of results rather than the trend, so that early evolving DIC is missed
interpreting a normal fibrinogen as reassuring when it is in fact falling from a high baseline as an acute phase reactant
giving prophylactic component therapy to correct numbers in a non-bleeding patient rather than treating the cause
overlooking the chronic compensated form that presents with thrombosis, so anticoagulation is withheld inappropriately
failing to search actively for and treat the precipitating disorder
references: British Society for Haematology guideline on the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation
management: Treating the underlying trigger such as sepsis, obstetric emergency, malignancy, trauma, pancreatitis, or burns is the single most important intervention
Replace components guided by bleeding and by trends, giving platelets, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate for hypofibrinogenaemia
Use therapeutic heparin anticoagulation where thrombosis predominates and bleeding risk is low
Consider physiological anticoagulant support such as antithrombin in selected cases
Provide supportive organ support for microvascular thrombosis and multi-organ dysfunction
Monitor serially with platelet count, prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times, fibrinogen, and D-dimer, interpreting the trend rather than single values
Involve haematology early and, in obstetric DIC, undertake urgent delivery or evacuation of the uterus
